blocks.x: From a child. Pardon me, you said you... My first good inspiration of music was taken from that French opera house. Did you go there? How often did you go about? Oh, weekly. Every weekend. And on Sunday night and eight I used to go there. And pretty much all the operas that are not played today, I've seen a great many operas.
A lot of the old French operas, I guess. Like the Huguenots, you mentioned, they don't have that today much either.
Oh, La Favorita, Jerusalem, La Juive. Yes. And... O'Dalda Jha.
I collect opera programs. I have quite a few old French opera programs.

The Prophets. By the way, talking about The Prophets. On a concert that I directed at Xavier University, it was in the month of December, I think, of 1932. I had a group, an orchestra. And speaking about this opera, The Prophets, we played The March for The Prophets. As the first number on that program. I'll never forget that. Was that by Meyerbeer?
By Meyerbeer. I think I have the program of that opera, at the French Opera. And...let's see...

I'm sorry I didn't get it out. But I have the program of that concert... Someday, maybe we can come back sometime and look over those. I have the program of that concert. Well, I directed that program. That's it. And it was quite a success. Now, myself, I had to make some substitute on that occasion. We didn't have any French horns. We didn't have no bassoons. We didn't have no oboe. But this is what I did. We had an orchestra of 26 pieces. I used a C clarinet, besides the first and second B flat. Yes. Yes. I used a C clarinet as a no-go. And I used a C tenor saxophone and a B flat bass clarinet as bassoons. As bassoons, yeah. And I used two mellophones. French horns. French horns. French horns. French horns. But otherwise, I had a set up. I had a cello. I had bass. I had viola. I had first and second violins. I had two clarinets. I had two flutes. I had two trumpets. I had two trombones. And drums. And it came out pretty good, of course. Sometime I think it could have been better, but it seemed to be appreciated by the... Some of them are students. Dillard students, I guess.
Some of them had been students of Xavier. I thought I mean Xavier. That was given out to Xavier or Dillard? Xavier. Xavier. Yeah, that's what I meant. That was given out Xavier. That was December 32.

Yeah. And of course, like those fellows would be the... Now as far as jazz is concerned, I used to play a lot of jazz on the piano, you know? Oh yes. But I never did fancy very much of piling up in those... the red light districts. I never said to go around there. I didn't want to worry about that at all. Although, much of my colleagues used to play. Piku and all of them used to play.
Professor Minetta's told us about those. He played at the tuxedo dance hall and some of the houses and all too. Yes. Yes. He's told us all about that. But I used to play for private people.

Private dancers I used to play. And I had a whole set of... a whole set of dances. During those ten days, they used to have a certain order of dances, you see? They start off with a waltz, you see? Then they did a polka, you see? Then a mizooka, then a shardis. They used to dance those kind of dances before and then come back to a polka and repeat that. And then they would have a waltz and quadrille. And when the waltz was danced, as the rule, the dancers used to get their partner for the quadrille to make sure that they had their set. And after the quadrille, why then the orchestra would go to supper and they'd come back and wanted to go over that same routine again. Well, I had that routine down pat and I used to play all those things on the piano. I used to play for private affairs. And by doing so, I remembered a lot of the areas of that time. Especially the quadrille areas. And it so happened when Miss Senegal...
I heard about it. You organized the group for the Creole Festival? I organized the group for the quadrille. Now I'm going to tell you how that happened.

I wasn't acquainted with Miss Senegal. But I heard of what her intention was to portray the amusement of the 90s. What made up the general pleasure of those times. And she wanted everything that could have happened at that time. So she was in the waltz for her quadrille. She didn't know where to find a quadrille. She knew to dance the quadrille and so it was a favorite dance at the time. And she wanted a quadrille of the old areas of that time. But at that time, my sister, she's passed away too. She passed away now. Next month will be two years. She had a group at Holy Redeemer's Church on Royal Street. Of old people. And they used to give old folks concerts. All them old people. They used to sing those songs and dance and go on. And it was a real pleasure for the folks that would go on. And they would do it for the benefit of the church. You see. And Miss Senegal heard of it. And she contacted my sister. And I said, my sister, if she knew. And so my sister told her, well, my brother remembers a lot of those areas. She would contact him. She said, well, tell your brothers to come and see me. So I went out to Miss Senegal and I visited her and I told her that I could help her along that line. Oh, she was so glad. So what I did, I sat down and from memory, I jotted down the quadrille using areas that was used for quadrille at that time. You see. Who were they composers? I don't know. Where was the music? I don't know. She had tried all over the city, couldn't find it. She went to Piku and all of them. The last man that I knew had the music, well, he was dead a long time. He's been dead now. Oh, he's been dead over 40 years ago. And the music disappeared. I have some of them. But I used my memory and jotted down. And then I said, well, now I could orchestrate that just like on the order of that time. I said, but today they're using, they wasn't using no saxophone at that time. They were using second violin, not guitar. So I gave it as much as the old time idea, you understand? But with a tinge of modern musician and I raised it. Then I went to Pajot, my poor friend, who's always there. And I told Pajot about it and I got him interested. So after I got him interested, I briefed him on the thing and the Senegal was in war for dances. And there was nobody that she could remember that danced to Pajot real. And she got some old folks that used to dance and had forgotten it. But I and my sister had remembered the set and for a number of rehearsals from November, I might say. So from November 53 all the way to August 54. At regular week, real rehearsal. I finally taught them the steps and taught them the whole thing. And made it possible for her to produce that choir trail. And they are all the tour in the square there.
I missed that. I wasn't in town then. I saw some of those Creole festivals. Once went Piku and Celestan different people played. But about three years.
So they started playing on that program, on that program. And there was two nights of it then. Which year was that? 54? 54. I was there in 55.
Oh, 55. And 53 the year before. But not that year. I missed that.
Well for reasons better known for myself and of course I didn't hear her card. And I wouldn't go into details about that. But we fell out.
She had another group on the boat, you know, about three years ago.

Well she tried to dance the choir trail after that. But she didn't even remember the step that we taught. I wish I had seen your... I still have. I still have that old choir trail here. She tried to get it from me and so forth. She tried to have it televised but she wanted to televised on her own.
Yes, they put it on television but only about one minute of it. Just so little you could hardly see what it was like.
Well what you saw on television was not the real thing at all. Not the real thing. And it wasn't the music either because I had...
No, Paul Barberin tried to arrange something for her.
Well they played to arrange something but that wasn't the music at all.
So I can believe that.

Because I had the music here and I had this copywriter. And that's where she wanted to take the thing in charge. And when I explained to the WDSU, Mr. who was in charge then? The poor fellow that apprehended the commons or something.
Boy I remember his name begins with L. I can't remember now what it was. Liberalite.

That's it. Well, well he explained that they could use it as commercial and so forth. And after she got through speaking, I spoke to Mr. and I told him, I just got it up. I said, it's a memory of 50 years ago. I was quite a boy when those pieces were being played. And being of a mind of, you know, I can, you can play something today and I can get up tomorrow morning and whistle it. And I would come pretty near having the division exactly like it was. Although, as you know, you can sing a song, you can hear a song and sing it. And anybody would know that you're singing that song.
But if you were to write it down like you see, you see the division wouldn't be just quite the same division as a bigger musician.
A lot of times. A bigger musician you ought to know that. But I could come pretty near making the same division that I heard. It's been a thing with me ever since my childhood.
Good talent to have.

Yeah. And I remembered, I remembered those arias from that time. And all I did was sing them and jot them down because usually when I do any writing, very seldom I use the piano. I use my solfege, you know, in writing the intervals, you know. Just do it by, in your head then. Yeah. And so I picked the chorus. Now I picked it very nice. And what was nice about it, the boys all liked it. I put a clarinet variation. I put a clarinet variation that this fellow around the corner on Claymore Street, you know him. He's a clarinet player. He's a playing musician today. Dillard Rhodes. He has a shooter tying place like that. I'm trying to think.
Yeah. And I know him. Well. Well, do you know him?
He played the clarinet part on that occasion. And he even came here and wanted to look over it. Well, I wrote that clarinet variation too. Is he still alive, Mr. ?
Who's alive? Mr. Belrose, is he still alive? Belrose? What's the name again? Oh, he's a young fellow.

He has, him and his brother has a shoemaker shop, a shoe repair shop right around on Claymore, here, Ursuline. Well, he was the one that played on that occasion, you see. And he liked the variation so much he came here.

He's a pretty good clarinet player too. I have some of the old piano, the sheet music to some of the old quadrilles that I pick up now and then. But I never did get any orchestrations of them. No, that's what I'm telling you. The orchestrations were gone. At one time did they sell the orchestrations too? Was I? At one time when you were young, did they have the orchestrations for sang-al-tino on those quadrilles?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. They didn't buy all of them. Yeah, but it's all out of date. It's always way past the, it's way past the public domain as the copyright. That's right, the expired domain. And I even, in copywriting it, I even had to tell the copyright officers, of course, they ask you who were the composers, and who was the artist and so forth. I had to tell them I didn't even know who the composers were. And I don't even remember seeing the music, looking at the music itself. But it was just that I remembered the area and I placed my own arrangement.
Yes, you can always copyright your own arrangement, of course.

Well, that's what I did. I got my own arrangement copyrighted, you see. And, oh, it went on nice, it went on nice. We should sing that. Yeah. And I was fixing to get the boys together, because I, very few musicians I know now, they all, you're all my old musician friends, they're all gone. I suppose. Yeah, I remember, I remember, I remember, I remember, I remember, I remember, I remember, and Peter Brokaw, and about some of the only ones that I can remember back that time, you understand? I, I, I don't know of any other of the old musicians. Of course, that was Papa Celestine, but I remember when he came here, when Papa Celestine first came here, and we played with the, uh, uh, Tuxedo Band, which he still kept that name, Tuxedo Band. And, B.B. Ripley was the first organizer of that Tuxedo Band. Well, I played with them, they all played, I played with them all, I played with them. Oscar Randall used to have a band, I used to play with him. And, uh, there's another fellow, I forget his name, the last band I played with. But, all that's over 30, 35 years ago, you know what I mean? And I stopped playing out and so forth. When did you stop about? Oh, I, I stopped playing as far back as the, uh, a lot of part of the twenties. I, I mean, playing out here. No, that's your plan. I kept my little playing here, and I grew up in the horse with my friend, uptown, uh, Mr. Chalice. He has a musical family, Chalice has a musical family, and, uh, they all play music. And, used to go up there, and, I still go up some time. Since my wife died, well, I don't get around so much, but I used to go up there and play with them, you know, and so forth. And now since authorized, I've been getting a hold of my fingers, it's kind of difficult. Yeah, so I don't, I don't have to touch the piano now anymore.
And, uh, I was gonna ask, when did you start to work for the post office? I started to work for the post office in 1906.
That far back? June the 2nd, 1906. And I retired on this, on January the 1st, 1952. Were you a mail carrier most of that time? Well, I worked as a carrier, I worked as a 22. I worked as a 22.
I didn't see how anybody's feet and legs could hold up that long. Yeah, there you are, there you are. You got around well, though. Yeah.

And, uh, well, I retired, yeah. I had 45 years and seven months. And, uh, would be able to still go on. But, uh, had it not been that, uh, I understood that, uh, if I had continued working, I'd be working for nothing. That's right, yeah. Because, you see, there's a certain portion out of your salary is taken for your- Social Security and all that. For your pension, not Social Security. Oh, that pension.
Oh, that pension.

But, uh, it makes no difference how many years you stay there. If the amount of years amount to a pension that will be more than 80% of what you're actually getting, you couldn't get any more than 80%. That's right, yeah. So, when I saw that the amount of years I had was reaching the 80%, you understand, and if I'd continue working, well, I'd be putting in the funds, putting in the funds money that I would never get back. Yes. You see, I would- It wouldn't benefit me any of getting any more pension. Of course, it would much well- Yeah. That's why I left.
Oh, I was gonna ask a little bit more about the French Opera. If you can tell us some more about-

Well, as I was saying, we played, uh, Rubichaud played for the Els de Rondre on that yacht. I forget just what year it was. But it was, uh, either one or two years, or three possibly, before the opera boy. And, uh, Rubichaud got an orchestra, he drew upon all the good musicians that he could. And he had an orchestra of 30 pieces, 30 or 36 pieces, something of that sort. And I played, I played cello on that orchestra. Piro and all the musicians, Gaspar, and all of them, Charlie McCurdy, Bloom, and all of them. We played on that occasion. And in order to, uh, get ourselves set, because our orchestra was placed in the second tier. Well, you were up above. In the second tier, you see. The stage, the platform for the dance was covered from the stage, covering the pocket all the way back. Oh, yes. You see? Now, the first tier, or the amphitheater, was where the guests, the guests for the ball sat, you know? Oh, yes. I found out on that occasion, I used to think everybody danced, but on those balls, you know, there's invitees that come there, but they're not called out. Yeah, but they're not called out. They're not called out. There's only certain dancers that are called out by the masochist dancers. Well, I learned all that on that occasion when I played there. And, uh, this amphitheater was arranged for the invitees that, uh, just come to witness the ball. And the second tier, then, above, that came just above, was where the orchestra was placed that gave the music right down to the place, you see. So we went there on the Sunday, the Sunday before the, uh, it was, uh, one week, one week and two days before Mardi Gras itself. Because I believe the ball was to take place some night in that week. So we went there to rehearse and to find out just how we were going to sit. And being a youngster, you know, our youngsters already will pry around. I had the occasion of going all over that French opera. And I'm here to tell you this. For a building that was erected as far back, I believe it was, uh, 1859. Yes, I think that's right. 1859. And my mother's father worked on that building. My mother is dead now. She died in 28. And she was 90 years old when she passed away. And, uh, she always, she was the cause of us taking up with the opera because that was all her amulet. She remembered French opera before the French opera was built. Even before then. Yeah. The opera used to be, you know where the companies on Arlene Street? Yes. The, uh, the, uh, yeah, St. Bergman's. Yes. Well, that was called, uh, Thiat d'Orléans.
That's what I've heard of.

And that's where, that's where the, uh, the opera was. You see? And when they built this new opera, uh, I don't know what took place, but it burnt down. And when it burnt down, it remained a lot there. And, uh, I remember I was a little child. I remember seeing, uh, uh, an acrobat by the name of a Frenchman. Baptiste Pignot. He died from that, from a tower they had there and broke his neck. I witnessed that because my father held me on his shoulder. I must have been a little child then about three, four years old. But I still remember that. You still remember that? Yeah. And he was boarding, he was boarding at my wife's grandmother on St. Peter Street. I learned that afterwards. When my, when my wife showed me some pictures that her grandmother gave her, of this very same acrobat. And it all came back to me. He boarded with her grandmother. That's, that's something to remember. Yes, that's a good memory. So, uh, as I was saying, well, on that occasion when we were to pray for the Elvibobrio, we went down there, and I went all over. And the different apartments, you wouldn't think it was built so modern. There were parlors for men, parlors for women, and the cushions on the floor, the coffees on the floor. There was lounge room, there were poker rooms, and I even went to the top, where the top lights were. Now, back of stage, let me tell you about back of stage. On each side, one for men, one for women, there was a row of dressing rooms, you wouldn't imagine. A row of dressing rooms for all the choristers and so forth, on each side of the stage. Now, back of the stage, I never saw a stage of that sort. The sceneries for all the different operas were back of the stage, with enough room, that a grand display of an opera would have room in front. Now, the thing that they claim, I read after that, because they made an attempt to fill it over again, you know. I believe some of the people who used to describe to the office, people like Ms. Benjamin, and Ms. Jake Newman, and those people, you heard of them. Well, they got together, they wanted to build it again, but unfortunately they had a foreman, a chairman, that squandered the money away, somewhere, or other. But, however, well, under that stage, they claimed that it was a man here that had the, uh, reputation at that stage. There were trap rows underneath there. It was all wood, with, uh, pegs and ropes. Now, they could lower, anywhere in the stage, they could lower a square. A certain section. A certain section. And the top of it, the top of it used to slide over, you see. Yeah. But they slide that thing back, and, uh, they could bring that thing down, and bring it up that way, anywhere in the stage. And, uh, it was made that way for the purpose of certain operas. Now, I remember seeing one opera. It was called, uh, we brought a job, they say, call it. You know, it means to say something about the devil. And, uh. Robert the Devil. Robert the Devil, I saw that too. When, when they, they use those traps. Mm-hmm. You'd see the spirits come up from under the stage. And whenever they played Faust, whenever they played Faust, Yeah.
That's the devil. That's the devil.

That's the devil. That's the devil. That's the devil. That's the devil. That's the devil. That's the devil. That's the devil. That came from understated. You know, you're a big pool of five, and he's come right up. Mm-hmm. Like that. But now they, they don't know he comes from back in scenery. Yep. Because they don't have a stage like that. But a stage like that, I don't know if they'll ever be able to construct a stage with that stage. Well, I had the opportunity to witness and all that. When did the orchestra pit? Mm-hmm.
How big an orchestra did they usually have for the opera?

Well, I'll tell you, the orchestra pits they have was an orchestra of anywhere from 36 to 40 pieces, I think. Sometime it was more about that. Yeah. Yeah. They had an orchestra about, and they used to have an impresario that went away from me. I suppose you've been told that. I've read a little bit about those.
I've read a little bit about those.

I went away to Europe, and he'd pick up a troupe here. And there were certain musicians that lived here, that came here formerly with an opera company, that stayed here, and they were always signed up. Right. They were always signed up for when the orchestra would come and play. And this man, initially, Scott was his name. He was born in Toulouse, France, and he got his first education there. And he had his musical education in France, in Paris Conservatory. And he studied in Myron, Michigan. And he was, I believe, the chief cellist in that office with a kid. Because they always had, they always used three or four cellists, you know. Oh, yeah. And I got acquainted with him for Mr. Beaufort. Now Beaufort is a man that taught my friend trombone, Benny Raytheon. And when Benny used to go for his lesson, I used to go with him, you see. And we got well acquainted with him and so forth. And after he died, he had a little wine place on Charles Street. Not very far from where he lived. Between, I think it was between Toulouse and Madison. You know that little place there. And after he died, well, his wife kept it in place. So in later years, she opened the ballroom on Charles, between St. Louis and Toulouse, on the Riverside. And I was coming from the post office with me and my friend, Mr. Charlemagne, and all musicians, Mr. McNeil. And we was coming along and she was standing outside and she recognized me. Oh, she said, the friends of my old husband, she said, come right on in. So she took us back in that dining room because at that time, the law had changed. We either had a barroom for white or for colored. Well, in that neighborhood, she couldn't think of having a barroom for colored. There was no colored people around there. And so she has to say, well, you come right in and come back in my dining room. So we used to go back in the dining room. And in the afternoon when we used to leave, we used to pass there. We'd go back there and have drinks and everything else. We used to like to drink. You know how young fellas are. And so forth. And the opera, when the opera was there, all the musicians used to go there. She being a Frenchman herself, you understand? And she had an adopted son. She had no children. Oh, she had an adopted son. His name was Paul, like me. And Paul used to come back there. And they used to come back there and we all used to drink and go on. And that's why I met Mr. Lescar. He was interested in me because, of course, you know those fellas, they won't take any people unless you have some kind of a background. Well, he gave me a quiz and everything else and so forth and so forth. And he says, you've been well instructed. I said, well, it's nothing like being well instructed anyway. So he was stopping at Miss Vignard on St. Louis near Boyville. And I went there for lessons. I took lessons with him there. He taught me the cello. I had already taken some lessons with Professor Dickerson. But he taught me all over again. And I took lessons with him. And he began to give me, he was a harmonist too. He began to teach me a harmony when he had to leave. You see, he left. So that's why I went to Mr. T. O. And Mr. T. O. taught me all over again. And of which, you know you never get through.
No, I guess not in composition and harmony and all that.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I'd like to get some more right now if I could. I often thought that if I could get a hold of someone. Well, some of these professors around here, they teach people. I want to get a hold of a real good man, you know. And I don't care if I live to be a hundred years old. I'm going to study music. That's most of my music now. I study music. I have a book on harmony. I have a book on counterpoint and form. Well, I go along with that. And I have a friend that's eager to, a fellow by the name of Pritchard. You heard of that? Oh, yes. Well, he's the only man like myself that seems to be interested. These musicians, they don't care about it. As long as they can get out and gibba-dibba-dibba.
Yeah, make a little money and they can play for a dance. That's all they do.

But I'll tell you what I'm doing though. I have a composition that I'd throw on the side. I'd throw that composition on the side because at that time I didn't think anything of it. But you see, T. K. Huerta called man, he had a brother by the name of Uris. A singer. He had some kind of a band. He used to go around, a little routine band. I never got to know him.
I'm sorry. I always... Well, he died too. Yes, I heard about him.

Right here in the next block. You happen to be right in the neighborhood where these things took place. In the next block, the Claiborne hardware store bought out two Devil Cottages on Robinson Street to extend their business all the way through from Robinson to Claiborne. Well, those two Devil Cottages, Piku's mother lived in one of them at the time. And a friend of mine, Jean-Marie, his mother lived there. And on account of coming there with him, I found out that Piku's mother was living there in the neighborhood. Yes. Now, next door to Piku, there was a lady that was really friendly with her and had a piano. And when they found out that I'd come around there with my friend and say, well, come play. In those days, it was a great thing to go there and you'd play, they'd dance, they'd sing, you understand? And make a supper and so forth, and that was entertainment, you know? That was much entertainment. So I used to go off the road. . . .
Well you imagine that Pinker's brother is full of jokes you say?
Yeah, and those people were Creole people and they spoke as much Creole as they did English, maybe more.
I knew his brother would sing a lot of Creole songs.

Yeah, well that's what I'm coming to. And he said, I'll have to translate it for you because he said it in Creole. It means, who told you I was going there? I told him nobody said you was going there. I told him in French, nobody was going there. And from that, I just started and started to play with a little tune you know. I'll compose myself. And from that we made a song. You see? And the song goes like this in Creole. It says, who told you I was going there? It speaks as though two people were talking, two friends. Who told you I was going there? The other fellow answered, nobody told me you were going there. Yes, somebody told you I was going there. He said, no, nobody told me you was going there. Well how you come to know that I was going there? It was you who told me you was going there. No, I never told you I was going there. Yes, you told me I was going there. And I put it on you. And I framed it up that way, you see? But Pinker's brother only said, who told you you was going there? I thought a while and I made the song out of it. I threw it on the side and never worried about it. Today I realized that that kind of stuff goes.
Yeah, that's right. Some of those things would sell good now. They could make up the stuff.

Those things sell good. So I'm writing it. I'm writing it. And I don't know whether I orchestrate it or not because it's so hard to get an orchestra to. I like to have an orchestra to go over my way to see if I forgot something or if I want to put in something. Sometimes I might want to improve the phrase here or there. I might want to change the harmony just a little bit or place or another. You understand? Or I might want to put some little extra pep to it and so forth. Well, I was thinking about fixing that thing up. And there's another old tune that we used to play. It was never written. It was only a bi-tune. You know, like people make up a little tune. Oh yeah. And the band used to play. The old Spanish fort. Well, way back then when Matthew Perez was just beginning to play trumpet. I remember that as well. He was playing with a young boy that was a good violin player. I forget what his name was. Big Gasper and all of them, they were young musicians at the time. You know what I mean, playing. I was a kid. I was a little kid. I used to go out there for picnics and so forth. And they used to play a piece they called, Down in the Tin Cup Room. I know you didn't know that. Down in the Tin Cup Room. But it was only a ghost song. It was just somewhat of a Volcker song, you know?
Yeah. Some of those were, I know.

Some of the words. Yeah, and they used to sing around the red light district and so forth. But I figured on revising it and using it, not in that way, but using the idea. Down in the Tin Cup Room where I used to go, when they knocked me to the floor and took all my dough. I'm going to fix it up that way, you see? Yes. And that gives it to my heart. Remember all of them? In fact, that was never written. I'm going to write it down. Yeah, but nobody wrote that down at all, I guess. And I'm going to take them two pieces. I'm going to take them two pieces. But the only thing that I would like to get, and I was thinking very hard, there's only one person that I figured could sing better. And that's Lizzy Mahoney.

You know, Lizzy says she's not going to sing anymore now. No? Yeah, I saw her about three weeks ago and she said she wants to retire. And she's going to devote her time to the church. You know, she's been very religious. Oh yeah, I know because my wife was very religious.

And my wife used to meet her in church all the time. Really? I know her. I'm not personally acquainted with her. But I found out where she lived and I was just trying to go out there, pay her a visit. And knowing that she used to sing those creoles for her, I thought maybe I could...
Well, she could still sing.
I know.
Maybe she'll decide to go back sometime. You know, people change their mind.
If she would do it just in my interest, if she would water, I don't know, because she'd be able to put it over good.
Yes, she could then.
I know because of some of these days and Papa, won't you please come home and all. She found a way of...
And she made a good translation of them. Yeah, she sings a nice in Creole. I don't know the Creole.

I know the Creole language. And she has reproduced those songs so well in Creole that I don't think anybody could beat her. No. And she would be just the one to sing that La Basque song for me. At least she would. Yeah.

Well, maybe she'll change her mind. She goes to church every day, several hours she says now. Yeah. In the morning until afternoon sometime. And two weeks ago NBC was down. Some men from television in New York were down. They were going to put on a ragtime program or something and some old songs. And she wouldn't even talk to them about going to make any more television programs or anything. She didn't want to do it. That's too bad. But maybe she'll change her mind. I hope she does and sing your songs. Because I don't know anyone else.

They're real good. They're real good. And in fact, if a person doesn't understand the Creole, of course it jives better when you hear the Creole and can understand it. I suppose, yeah. Because there's two fellows. And they actually, it seemed as though there was something that the two of them was interested in. But you never know where that guy is. You know what they're talking about. Who told you you was going there? I didn't see you was going there. Yes, you told me where there is, you never know. You know. It's a guess, you see. That's some foolishness. That would mix it all together all the more catchy, you know. Yeah. And well, these other, I don't know who it was. You know, the others take it and they start it with a la ba. You know. Well, I suppose they must have stolen it from Piku because he went to speak about the la ba. But that's not the la ba at all. The real tune of the la ba, I'll tell you how the melody goes. I can show you.
I can show you this melody. Yes. That's the way it goes. That's the way it goes. You see.

That's what it goes, you see? You know how it is with the bands of today, they take a separate piece and they make their own improvisions on it. They make their own improvisions. And I know the minute they get a hold of that, you see, they started making the improvisions on it out of this world and I know it to make it.

Albert Burbank sings the A La Ba very well, you know, the other A La Ba. And D.D. Pierce used to sing that a lot, a trumpet player. I never heard of it, how they sing it. It's just A La Ba. That's the one, yeah. Not like the one you played.
That's the original one that I composed. And it's fall back, let's see. That happened anywhere between 1912, between 1910 and 1914.

Anywhere along that time. Right in the next block right here. And then they sing the stars more like over there, A La Ba, A La Ba. And then, you know, they get into a lot of fast. I don't know all the Creole. I couldn't sing it.

No, but that's the original, you see? That's the original La Ba, you see? And I threw it on the side, never worried with it. Until you're late. I noticed, in fact, since my wife died, I noticed that a lot of that kind of stuff is going big. I said, well, why do you stay there? Why do you go? Well, I'm going to fix it up. Get it copyrighted. It'd be nice to try to do it. And if you know anyone, if you could advise me to anyone that I could see that would advise that you get it recorded and so forth, you know?
I'd appreciate that very much. If I think of somebody that would be interested, I certainly would let you know them.
And in other days, I have here so many different little areas that I've made myself, but just threw them on the side.

Well, I was going to ask a little bit, the other night you were telling about Piron when he first started in the publishing business. If you could tell us a little about that, if you remember? Well, Piron. I had a little more to talk to.

Piron. I met Piron out at Blooms. I'm telling you, with the office, I'm telling you about at Blooms. He played in the office and so forth. He became good friends, musicians, and so forth. And when he had a barbie shop there on Cravon Street near Columbus, right near Stewart was where the Musicians Union is. And he had a lot of boys, a lot of our boys friends were to come there. And there was a fellow by the name of Freddie Kemper. Not Freddie Kemper. Let's see. I can't even go on, I'm saying Freddie Kemper. That's the old trumpet player, not him. It was a Clarence Williams, a piano player. Wait a minute, wait a minute. This boy is not a musician.
Freddie Ratlin.

Oh, I never knew about that. I know you've never knew about that. Freddie Ratlin wrote a song. What is this world to me? You see, what is this world to me? And he wrote the words. And he told Pirol, can you put that to me over? So Pirol composed an area up there. And Pirol came to me and said, you think you could do that? Because I used to play piano with Pirol privately in different places, you know. He used to play piano before he met Williams, before he met George Williams. And I wrote it in a compliment. You see? I arranged it. And we both grew in together. We had it in prison. We wrote it in . We had about 50 or so copies made, and so forth. And we showed it among our friends. And unfortunately, it got away from me. I never reserved a copy of it. Yeah. Well, that was Pirol's first composition. First round. And that was my first arena. That happened around that same time, 1911, 1912, somewhere around that time. And later, he met Williams. And his own song that he used to play with his officer, Brown Skin, he decided to get that guy. You see? He got that down and they made an arrangement for it and so forth. And he wasn't big with Clarence Williams. And he said, I'm not going to do it. And I was busy working in the post office and so forth. He never consulted me. So it just went that way. So it means this fellow, Jean-Marie, he wrote songs. So Jean-Marie wrote a song. And I put music to it. You understand? I'll hand up here. I believe I have one copy of that one. We published that together. Where's all the presents that you promised me? It's the right time song. I'd possibly take it and record it. But I never did anything with it before. I started making copies of it like I did before. And it's in public domain now. It's past the-
Past the 28 years, 56 years. You didn't renew it, I guess.

No. I didn't renew it. I didn't renew it. It's in the public domain. Then I put music to another piece that Jean-Marie wrote. It was called Jailhouse Blues. And we found out that somebody else had a Jailhouse Blues. Yes. Bessie Smith made one of the record. Then we have- Then he wrote another one, Lloyd Babe. Lloyd Babe. And I put music to that. And there were several other pieces. There were orchestrated for it. And I got a- I got a- I got a- Chase them up there. I got a lot of music there. I got both classical and jazz and everything else. I got a lot of music. I- Yeah. I don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don't- Don- But I kept up with that theory of music, you understand? Most so. I got interested in that, and I got interested in interpreting pieces, you know, like conducting orchestras and things like that. And I did more of that in recent years than before, than in doing any playing. And then, unfortunately, I lost my cello. I had a cello that was an heirloom from my mother's family. I don't know why it came. And that was the instrument I learned on. Unfortunately, my friend Mike Neal, the one that I spoke before, was living on Durban Street near the Maine. And when we were playing for Robe Show, we used to rehearse at his house. And his daughter, his oldest daughter, seemed to have taken a liking to the cello. And he asked me would I let the girl use the cello? Well, I let her down. And he had a big fire when nobody was home, and the cello got drunk. Well, it burned up. And I stayed without a cello. Oh, I don't know how long I stayed without a cello. That happened way back then. Which season? Somewhere around 1922, 23. And I stayed without a cello until a friend of mine had a cello, but I don't fool it up because it's, I don't like the tone of it, because it's a school cello. And it seemed as though this man was a friend of a friend of mine. And he wanted to borrow $25. And he gave the cello as a horse. But he never did pay the $25. He never kept with a cello. So my friend gave the cello to me. In fact, he sold it to me. I paid him for it because I had been with a cello so long. So I thought it best to take that or not. I wasn't in a position to go buy an instrument. Because to buy an instrument like I'd want would be very expensive. You know, a cello is not a cheap instrument. So I have it there. And I have my saxophone there. That was made a present to me by my wife, the saxophone. And my whole clarinet is there.
You still play the Albert? Did you ever change over to the Bain system? No, no, no.
But I suppose it's easier enough. I understand how it works.

I know how it works already enough. But even if you know how it works, it requires practice. Yes, that's right. I was going to ask some more. The Teos all played Albert's system, I guess. Did they the old men do? Yeah.

Even worse than that. I remember the Louis Teo telling me, he said, you lucky. You lucky to have a clarinet with 13 keys on you. You ought to play on a 10 key clarinet like I love you. 10? 10 keys. That key down there where you make seats, he said, you have to have a super little finger

to move from that hole to that hole. Ralph Collins here is learning clarinet. He takes lessons from Manuel Mineta on clarinet too. So he has a 13 key. He likes the 13 key better than the 15. Yeah. Yes, Albert.
Well, that's a clarinet. I learned 13 key clarinet.
You know, Professor Mineta teaches like Sam Dutre used to play, putting the upper lip on top of the teeth. Did you ever learn that way? No. That's the German.

That's the German. That's the German armature. You bite it? You bite it in your teeth? No, no, I play the French. I play the French, you see? I don't bite the ring, you see? You cover it. Up above, I don't put the teeth down. It's just a lip. Just a lip.
Well, that's what I mean. That's what Sam Dutre and Manuel Mineta teaches that right here.
To me, you get a rigid tone. Yeah, that's what he says.
And that's everything with a clarinet, you know? Of course, you can become proficient with the fingers, so agile with the fingers that you

can go forward with. You can play that tone that you have to cultivate until you get a reed that will just fit you to give that tone. Let's say we were an oboe. I have an oboe here, an old time oboe. I played a little bit of oboe. Not played out. In my head, a old time oboe, the keys were open on it. Right down there in the middle of it. Yeah, that's right. And I tried the flute, too. I played a little flute.
Do you still play a 13 key, Albert, Mr. Warner?
Well, if I was to play, I haven't checked a clarinet for years. But you have a 13 key. I have a 13 key clarinet.
Do you know about the T.O.'s, if they used that French system of covering the teeth?

No, I don't know. I think they did. I think they did. I've never questioned the particular amateur that they used. But I have reason to believe that they used the French. I don't know. I'm not saying that as a positive factor. I have reason to believe because the tone they got out of the clarinet was wonderful. In fact, any reading instrument, good to you, put the clarinet down, pick up the bassoon, give a rich tone, put that down, pick up the oboe, or the English horn. You see? He even played some instruments that I've never seen. He told me about them. There's a, there's an oboe d'amour. Oh, yes. There's an oboe d'amour, and there's, oh, several other reed instruments that he played. He played the English horn, and so forth. Oh, he was good at all the reading instruments. And best of that, he was, the Lord, you know, things like the old one, he was all papa. He was an accomplished conductor. Accomplished conductor. And he was good harmonious, common point, everything else. You know, you could take a little melody that long after you got through imitating and really make a, something back there. Yeah, make a development into something real big. Yeah, development into something real big. And that's what I, I can do a little of it, not much, but that's what I would like to do, to perfectionate myself. Yeah, imitation, fuge, loy teo, just like that.
From what I understand, he graduated from Big Honors in Mexico. Did he ever talk to you about Mexico, anything about down there? Well, he was, he was, that's one thing that was peculiar about him.

He was a drag and kind of talking to him, and very sensitive. He'd be afraid after you knew him, very afraid to say something that he'd be too sensitive about. Oh, well, just like that. So sometimes he'd be puzzled to question him.
Yeah, you wouldn't want to question him too, actually.

So I never got very much about that. The only thing I knew he used to speak about, he used to show me his old books of harmony, and tell me this and that and the other and so forth. And he could harmonize in any key you want, any key. And part is a soft way, you know what I'm saying? You could be singing here and you'd change key and everything else, he'd tell you the key you changed to. All he wanted to know, where you began. Yeah. He'd get, he'd get an idea of a keynote of what key you're singing in. He'd give it to him, where you gonna sing? Money. No. He'd get that tone. Now if it's C, alright. If it's C, call it C. Now you can go on and sing or you can go on and play, and you can modulate from any key. Every key modulates, you can tell you where you're going. Minor, major. He was a, he was an expert. Yeah, I bet he was. I regretted the day he died. But unpretentious. You know when he died about? I don't know. Or do you know if they have any of the family? Somebody told me that some of the relatives may be still living. I don't know. I don't know any of his relatives here. Of course, the young Lorenzo was married to one of the boatswain.

Bocage dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear

We called him Lanky, young teal. We called him Lanky. But he wasn't there. He wasn't an old man Lorenzo's only son. He had brothers and sisters. Maybe some more. They may be still over there in Basinless or Pasquale, whatever place you lived in Mississippi. They may be still there. Or even over here.
I believe there's one relative somebody told me about.

And they may be able to give you. Something about their life. About their life. I just knew them here. And you see that old fellow going along. He was somewhat humbucked. It's him going along with he had an old-time clown in his case. He'd go along with his clown in his case and so forth. He used to hang it around his shoulder. See, there goes old Lloyd Teo. No one ever knew what was that. It was really in his brain.
There was a lot of music up there.

Oh, indeed he was. He was one of the best we ever had. Him and old man Doc Moniz. And who was it? Galon Dufres. Doc Monique, his name. Doc Monique. Doc Monique. Doc Monique. What genus fruit did you find?
Fruit.

He was the one you told us about. Yeah. He was an excellent fruitist. And did they ever tell you about Alcibiad Jean-Jacques? No, I don't think so. Alcibiad Jean-Jacques was a corner player. I don't know who he studied with. He must have studied with one something Frenchman. Because most of them, they got from those Frenchmen that came there with the opera. He must have studied with them. And he went away with a show. And when he came back, I never knew him. I never heard him before he left. But when he came back, you're talking about a beautiful tone in a cornet. Oh, you know what the prettiest tones you want to hear. In fact, I can name you all the cornetists that had beautiful tones. You heard of George Moret? Yes. George Moret was a good start trumpet player and a good musician. But it's his brother you should hear. René Moret. He had a good tone. Sweet tone. And the one that played my good friend, Alon Metwiler. Yes. René Moret, Alon Metwiler, I told him. He was a little bit of what René Moret could do. He would do it to round the bar. He'd take his mouthpiece. You understand? You know that solo by Rossini, Inflammatus?
I don't remember. It's a religious song. I've seen the music. Yeah, I know what you mean.
You heard that.
Is that from the Stabat Madar or something? Stabat Madar.
From the Stabat Madar. Yes, that's it.
Yeah, I know.

I know what he did. He's mouthpiece along. And all you had to do is put through your ear there and you could recognize he was tonguing that very same piece. Just the mouthpiece along. Just with the mouthpiece along. To show you how much intonation that he had. Yeah. Well, he had a beautiful tone. Now, another person that had a nice tone was Charlie Dublé. He was before my time. And I remember him because when I first just got to be a friend when he died. And this is Jean-Jacques. And Valentino. You heard of him? No, I don't think so. Paul Kidd Valentin. Well, he studied. He specialized in trumpet. He studied in Mexico, too. He was a dentist. He lived here. Let's see. He died in California. But he lived here and went to Los Angeles. Because his wife died and he married another wife and so forth. He made my dentures. My plates. And he sold his house and he went to. But he was a solo Cornelis. And I'm telling you, he was that. Taps. Taps. You can take it from me. We used to call him Paul Kidd. Paul Kidd Valentin. His last name was Valentin. He was one of the fine Cornelis here. Well, this Jean-Jacques, I said, Jean-Jacques was equally a French hornist. And in the orchestra that I'm telling you about, that we played with Bloom and so forth, and I played the cello part. Well, he played French horn. And Barry Astuart, you heard of the Astuart?
I've heard of one clarinetist, I think, by that name. No, no, not that. No, no, no. I don't know.

I don't think you heard of them. Because the last one died, the youngest daughter, she was an accomplished pianist. No, I never knew. They had a brother that was a tromborist and a French horn. Well, that's the one of them. Well, his name was Barry Astuart. He played second horn in that orchestra. But Jean-Jacques played first horn. And we're talking about a man that had a lips that did. He'd never come to. It was once said that a person with a thick lips couldn't play a trumpet. They'd have to have thin lips. But you should hear either a trumpet or a French horn. And he was tops. He died two years ago. In fact, all of them were gone.
The real old musicians were all gone. Much like most of them are gone. All gone. Kiku is about one of the old. And then Kiku.
Kiku, a fellow like Kiku and like myself, we call ourselves young musicians outside of these people I'm talking about. Because when I was a kid, just coming up with boys, those people were men.
Oh, yeah. They were old enough.

Some of them were old enough to be my grandfather at that time. Yes. So you can imagine. But they were, I can't remember this much, they were top musicians. They wasn't amateur. They were professionals. Yeah. Is Kiku a little older than you? Oh, yes. Kiku is much older than me.
So I thought he's older.
I judge Kiku must be a man in his 80s.
Probably. He ought to be 80 probably. Yeah.
And I'm only at the beginning of my 70s. That's right.
You're still young. Compared to Kiku and Glenny and people like that. Oh, Glenny. He was 88, wasn't he? Something like that.
He must have been 88 or pretty young. I knew Albert Glenny.
Smart to go ahead.
Albert Glenny. I knew Albert Glenny since I was a baby. Albert Glenny was a great big man.

I knew him quite a long time, too. Yeah. Well, I was going to ask some more about the high society. Do you remember who composed it when you found the music? Because I found late arrangements of it. Even Clarence Williams put his name on it finally. I haven't got time.
I haven't got time.
Don't bother to look it up now. But someday.
I have it. I have it right here.
Someday if you find it. I wonder.
The one who composed, who is the author, composer of high society.

There was another arrangement I had, I think, published by Melrose in Chicago. But several people published it in late years. Yeah. And somebody published one called Porter and Stiegel. But just to think.

That piece had to come down here. And Robichaud had to try. And such people as, like I tell you, George Marquis, and Bad Frank, and finally P. Guhoud and others. Yes. And made that variation. Kindle that is known all over the United States. All over the world now. The world. It's a New Orleans tune. Yeah. It's a New Orleans tune from the fact that New Orleans made it famous. But it wasn't composed in New Orleans. It's going to show you how it came here. Yeah. I was told. I was told that tobacco was found here before it was in Havana. And today Havana tobacco is superior to American tobacco.
Yeah.
Irish potatoes would not engage with Ireland. Irish potatoes would walk to Ireland. Yeah.
Irish potatoes would not like to live in Europe.

I'm going to ask once more about the French Opera, if they ever gave any concerts there, like say solo recitals by piano players or the orchestra concerts, if symphonies there or was it always just opera?
Well, I believe they have had occasions when they had concerts there. Of course, I never attended none of them, but I tell you what, they didn't have there.

segments.chapter: Opera house and Creole dance traditions
segments.title: Hearing French opera as a child
segments.summary: Beaulieu says his first musical inspiration came from weekly visits to the French opera house; they list operas no longer performed.

segments.chapter: Opera house and Creole dance traditions
segments.title: Directing the Xavier University concert, December 1932
segments.summary: He recalls conducting a 26-piece orchestra at Xavier, playing the Prophet march and substituting clarinets, saxophone and mellophones for missing instruments.

segments.chapter: Opera house and Creole dance traditions
segments.title: Playing piano for private dances, not the red-light district
segments.summary: He says he played jazz piano but avoided the red-light districts, instead playing private dances with a fixed order of waltz, polka, mazurka and quadrille.

segments.title: Organizing the quadrille for the Creole Festival, 1953-54
segments.summary: He explains how Miss Senegal sought an old-time quadrille, how he wrote it from memory, recruited dancers with his sister, rehearsed them from November 1953 to August 1954, and then fell out with her.

segments.title: The television version of the quadrille was not the real thing
segments.summary: They discuss a brief TV broadcast of the quadrille that did not use his music, and his dealings with the station about it.

segments.title: Remembering tunes from fifty years ago and writing by solfege
segments.summary: He explains he can recall tunes from boyhood and write them down by solfege, almost without the piano.

segments.title: The clarinet variation written for Belrose
segments.summary: He describes writing a clarinet variation for the young player who performed it, and who now repairs shoes nearby.

segments.title: Old quadrille orchestrations and copyrighting his arrangement
segments.summary: They discuss lost quadrille orchestrations and sheet music, and copyrighting his own arrangement when composers were unknown.

segments.title: Old Tuxedo Band days and ceasing to play out in the 1920s
segments.summary: He recalls playing with the Tuxedo Band, Oscar Randall and others, stopping playing out in the 1920s and now playing occasionally with the Chalice family.

segments.title: Thirty-odd years at the post office and retirement
segments.summary: He gives his post office dates, 1906 to 1952, and explains he retired once his pension reached the 80 percent cap.

segments.chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
segments.title: Playing cello for Robichaux at an opera house ball
segments.summary: He describes Robichaux's 30-piece orchestra for a Mardi Gras ball at the French Opera, how the tiers were arranged, and his family's ties to the opera.

segments.chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
segments.title: Exploring the French Opera building and its stage machinery
segments.summary: He describes the opera house backstage, dressing rooms, trap system, the earlier burned theater and a childhood memory of an acrobat.

segments.chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
segments.title: Size of the opera orchestra and its impresario
segments.summary: In answer to a question, he says the pit orchestra had 36 to 40 pieces and that an impresario assembled troupes.

segments.chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
segments.title: Studying cello with the opera cellist and then Mr. Tio
segments.summary: He tells how he met a French opera cellist through a bar and ballroom run by his widow, took cello and harmony lessons from him, and later studied with Mr. Tio.

segments.chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
segments.title: Continuing to study harmony and counterpoint
segments.summary: He says he still studies music from books on harmony and counterpoint, unlike most musicians.

segments.title: The neighbourhood where Picou's mother lived and parties there
segments.summary: He mentions an old composition and recalls Picou's mother living nearby, and the house parties with piano and singing.

segments.title: Composing the Creole song 'Who told you I was going there?'
segments.summary: He explains how a remark by Picou's brother led him to compose a Creole song about two friends arguing.

segments.title: Reviving 'Down in the Tin Cup Room' and other old tunes
segments.summary: He describes unwritten old tunes he heard at picnics and in the red-light district, which he plans to rework and write down.

segments.title: Lizzie Mahoney as the ideal singer for his Creole songs
segments.summary: They discuss Lizzie Mahoney's Creole singing and her recent retreat into the church, and his hope she might sing his songs.

segments.title: His original 'A La Ba' and getting his compositions recorded
segments.summary: He distinguishes his original La Ba, composed about 1910-14, from other versions and asks for help to copyright and record it.

segments.title: Piron's first composition and the song 'What is this world to me'
segments.summary: He recalls meeting Piron at Bloom's, and arranging Piron's first composition with Freddie Ratlin's words around 1911-12.

segments.title: Jean-Marie's songs, theory and the loss of his cello
segments.summary: He discusses his songs with Jean-Marie, public domain status, his interest in theory and conducting, and the burning of his cello around 1922-23.

segments.title: Albert-system clarinets, embouchure and his other reed instruments
segments.summary: They discuss 13-key Albert clarinets, French versus German embouchure, and the oboe and flute he has tried.

segments.title: Lorenzo Tio's musicianship and harmony
segments.summary: He praises Tio's tone on reed instruments, conducting, harmony and ear, and says he knew little of his Mexico background.

segments.title: Tio family and what became of them
segments.summary: He says young Lorenzo Tio, called Lanky, had siblings who may still live elsewhere, and describes the old man walking with his clarinet case.

segments.title: Old-time flutists, cornetists and horn players
segments.summary: He recalls Doc Monique, Alcibiade Jean-Jacques, the Morets, Valentin and Barry Stuart, praising their tone.

segments.title: Picou, Albert Glenny and the age of the old musicians
segments.summary: They compare the ages of Picou, Glenny and himself, calling the earlier men professionals who seemed grandfatherly.

segments.title: Who composed 'High Society' and how it came to New Orleans
segments.summary: They wonder about the composer of High Society and he says Robichaux and others spread it, comparing it to tobacco and potatoes.

segments.title: Whether concerts besides opera were given at the French Opera
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about concerts at the French Opera, and Beaulieu says he never attended any.
